title: Suspending a compromised relayer zeroes every capability at once and hands operations to a standing backstop relayer
content:
A.6.1.1.3.2.6.1.2.2.2.3.1 gives the exact remedy: the Freezer Role *or* the Default Admin Role calls `manage_permission` with `status: PermissionStatus::Suspended` and every one of the nine capability flags set to `false`, "thereby preventing it from doing any further harm to the system. **The backstop Relayer can then take over.**" The guidance narrows the trigger: "this function should only be used if the keys to the Relayer multisig have been leaked or compromised, and the Relayer is now in the hands of an external bad actor."

That one sentence about the backstop retroactively explains the Prime Primary and Prime Secondary Relayer addresses. Redundancy is not merely about availability during key loss — it is what makes the suspension remedy usable. If Keel had a single relayer, revoking it during a compromise would halt all operations including the unwinding a crisis demands; with a second relayer already permissioned, the compromised key can be cut without stopping the machine.

Setting all flags false in addition to the suspended status is belt-and-braces: the status alone should suffice, but zeroing capabilities means no residual permission survives a later status change or a partial re-enable.

Note also that two roles can act here — the Freezer and the Admin — whereas restoring a relayer requires the Admin alone. The subtract-only asymmetry survives the platform change, and the narrow written trigger is the only thing distinguishing this emergency instrument from a routine way to switch operators.
description: manage_permission sets PermissionStatus::Suspended with all nine capability flags false; the guidance limits its use to leaked keys, and the secondary relayer then takes over.
